rich_summary: This section depicts the Pandavas overwhelming the forces of Jayadratha after the abduction of Draupadi. As the battle erupts, the five brothers fight with terrifying efficiency: Bhima smashes enemies and elephants with his mace, Arjuna cuts down hundreds with relentless archery, Nakula and Sahadeva slaughter warriors in close combat, and Yudhishthira himself kills a charging foe despite losing his chariot horses. The battlefield becomes a scene of carnage as armies collapse before them. Terrified, Jayadratha abandons Draupadi and flees into the forest. Draupadi is recovered and placed safely on a chariot, while Bhima begins hunting the fleeing king. Arjuna urges him to focus on Jayadratha rather than the retreating troops. Yet Yudhishthira reminds Bhima not to kill Jayadratha, invoking family ties through Dussala and Gandhari, introducing a tension between vengeance and restraint.

highlight_spans.why: A characterization of the Pandavas' righteousness and warrior code, establishing the moral framing of the coming battle.
The narrative shifts from warning to action as the five Pandavas surge into battle, darkening the air with arrows.
Bhima’s ferocity is displayed as he withstands volleys of weapons and crushes enemies and even an elephant with his mace.
Nakula’s dramatic duel with the charging elephant highlights individual heroism and martial skill.
Jayadratha’s panic and Draupadi’s recovery mark the emotional turning point: the victim is freed while the villain flees.

top_scenes.scene_text: Bhima, roaring in battle, swings his golden‑embossed iron mace and crushes an elephant and soldiers before Jayadratha’s chariot amid flying weapons.
Nakula leaps from his chariot and with a flashing sword severs the trunk and tusks of a charging war elephant as it collapses in fury.
Amid a battlefield strewn with fallen warriors and circling vultures, Jayadratha abandons Draupadi and flees into the forest while the Pandavas close in.
